Subject: Private VPC deployment: control plane proxy fabric & fallback plan

Hi Vivek,

Thanks for taking this on. We're kicking off the design review for a private VPC deployment of Redwood for our inference workloads. Key asks from our side:
- Support multi-tenant control plane routing (tenant-aware proxies) with per-tenant policy enforcement.
- Clear fallback behavior when dedicated capacity is exhausted (route to shared model variants or degraded QoS).
- Predictable egress IPs for SOC/audit whitelisting.
- Minimal changes to our current edge stack (we run k8s + Envoy at the perimeter).

Can you share an architecture sketch and run through any constraints you'd impose on us (natting, mTLS, cert rotation, required firewall rules)? Would be great to get a quick sync next week; we can invite our cloudops and security folks.

Attached: initial topology request template.

Best,
Michael Wallace
VP, Cloud Ops
Orion Financial Services

From: vivek.kulkarni@redwood.ai <vivek.kulkarni@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Private VPC deployment: control plane proxy fabric & fallback plan

Michael — thanks, this is a great summary.

High-level plan (I attached a quick sketched diagram):
- Control plane sits in a private subnet reachable by customer-managed proxies. We recommend a tenant-aware ingress proxy layer that routes to tenant-specific control-plane endpoints (no hairpin through public internet).
- Data plane (inference hosting) stays in a separate subnet with strict egress rules. Requests should use mTLS to the inference nodes; control plane traffic uses mutually authenticated TLS to the management endpoints.
- Fallbacks: when dedicated capacity is depleted we can route requests to a pre-approved shared model pool (quantized variant) with explicit degradation headers so your app can surface a graceful fallback.
- Egress: we can pin a small set of NAT IPs or provide a managed egress gateway in your VPC for audit whitelisting.

Proposed next steps:
1) 30-min design review (I can run through the diagram and constraints)
2) Customer network checklist (I'll send a short runbook)
3) Finalize SLA fallback behavior and test plan

I've attached: rwd-vpc-proxy-fabric-draft.pdf (diagram) — please review.

Availability: Tue/Wed next week 10–2 PT.

—Vivek
Vivek Kulkarni
Director, Solutions — Redwood Inference

Subject: Fwd: Private VPC deployment: control plane proxy fabric & fallback plan

Team — forwarding Orion's ask and my reply. Short notes / questions for the architecture review:

Context: Orion wants a private VPC layout that supports multi-tenant control plane routing (tenant-aware proxies), audited egress IPs, and fallback to shared model variants when dedicated capacity hits the cap. They run k8s + Envoy at edge.

Primary concerns I want to validate with you:
- Control plane / data plane separation: do we recommend one control-plane cluster per tenant or a shared multi-tenant control plane with tenant-aware routing? Tradeoffs on blast radius and onboarding.
- Proxy fabric: propose a thin per-tenant Envoy layer in customer k8s that does SNI + tenant header insertion and routes to our per-tenant endpoints (managed CRS). How do we handle TLS termination—bring-your-own cert vs. passthrough?
- Egress: Orion needs static egress for audit. Options: customer-managed NAT gateway with pinned IPs OR we run an egress appliance in their VPC (customer owned) that we talk to over peered link. Which is simpler for ops and SOC?
- Fallback semantics: header contract + metrics. We need a consistent header (X-Redwood-Fallback: variant=quantized, reason=cap) and a runbook hook.

Please reply with short bullet recommendations; I want to fold them into the design doc before the review.

Thanks,
Vivek
From: irene_choi@redwood.ai <irene_choi@redwood.ai>
To: vivek.kulkarni@redwood.ai, soojin_lee@redwood.ai, jonas_weber@redwood.ai
Date: Fri, 3 Sep 2027 09:26:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Fwd: Private VPC deployment: control plane proxy fabric & fallback plan

Quick notes from infra/security POV:

- Recommendation: shared multi-tenant control plane with strict per-tenant isolation at the proxy layer. Rationale: avoids operational overhead of per-tenant control-plane clusters while letting us enforce tenant isolation via access tokens and network ACLs.

- Proxy topology: customer Envoy should use TCP passthrough to our TLS front; we keep mTLS end-to-end to the control plane. This avoids cert management on their side while preserving client identity via SNI and a signed tenant header. If they insist on cert ownership, support it as an opt-in (BYO cert).

- Egress: require customer-provisioned NAT gateway(s) with pinned IPs. We'll support an alternate model where they deploy a lightweight rwd-egress-agent in their VPC that we can talk to over a private peering connection — useful for customers that cannot expose NAT IPs publicly.

- Network controls: avoid hairpin NAT (it increases latency and complicates traceability). For cross-AZ resilience, recommend at least two egress gateways in separate AZs behind a route53 weighted failover.

- Additional: KMS integration for tenant key wrapping; cert rotation cadence 30d recommended; provide an ops playbook for cert roll-forward.

Attaching a quick note on k8s annotations and Envoy listener config we should ask Orion to surface before the meeting.

—Irene
Irene Choi
Senior Network Architect — Redwood Inference

Michael — appreciated. Short summary of decisions and next steps (so we have a single source of truth before the call):

Agreed architecture decisions:
- Shared multi-tenant control plane with tenant isolation at proxy layer (Envoy passthrough to our mTLS front).
- Customer-provided NATs with pinned egress IPs recommended; alternative rwd-egress-agent + private peering supported for customers with stricter egress controls.
- Fallback behavior: X-Redwood-Fallback header will indicate variant and reason (example: X-Redwood-Fallback: variant=quantized-v2;reason=dedicated_capacity_exhausted). We'll provide templated SLA wording and a fallback annex for the contract.
- Ops: 30d cert rotation cadence; KMS integration for tenant keys; require two AZ egress gateways for resilience.
